newsitem.title: USA: US Airways briefs employees on its strategy.
newsitem.headline: US Airways briefs employees on its strategy.

text.p: US Airways Group Inc has called a family meeting, of sorts, to stress to its employees the need to cut costs, improve productivity and fight against mounting competition in the airline business.
US Airways, which has among the highest costs in the industry, this week launched a series of briefings with its employees to outline its financial and strategic position.

The Arlington, Virginia-based airline is at a crossroads. The company requires up to $1.5 billion in wage, salary and productivity concessions to bring its costs in line with other carriers, analysts said.

"They have a serious problem if they don't get the company fixed. They should be having superlative earnings in a year like this, but they don't. When there's an industry downturn, they will need to have addressed some of these issues," said Edward Starkman, an airline analyst with Dillon Read.
Some industry experts said the company could offer an employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) to its workers, giving them a stake in the company in exchange for the concessions.

The airline is seeking wage cuts up to 12.5 percent for its pilots at a time when their counterparts at rival carriers are seeking big pay increases. US Airways pilots want cost-of-living pay increases. Union sources said the two sides were moving towars a settlement, but progress has been slow.
"They've been very quiet about the talks. They have played this very close to the vest," said Susan Donofrio, an airline analyst with NatWest Securities Inc.

If the company was able to cut a deal with labor, US Airways could move ahead with its plan to acquire up to 400 Airbus Industrie aircraft, set up a low-cost carrier and possibly establish a stronger presence in the U.S. Midwest and outside the United States, analysts said.
With lower costs, US Airways could eventually become a prime acquisition target for airlines such as UAL Corp's United Airlines and AMR Corp's American Airlines, analysts said.

If US Airways was unable to strike a favorable labor settlement, it would be forced to shrink, analysts said. The airline would likely eliminate marginal routes and concentrate on areas where it could compete profitably, Timothy Ross, an analyst with SBC Warburg, said in a recent research report.
US Airways in its current form cannot counter the growing threat presented by low-cost carriers, analysts said.
"Where US Airways is currently exposed is its inability to counter the invasion of its natural markets by low-cost operators," Ross said.
"Until US Airways reaches some form of understanding with its unions...'no frills' airlines are likely to hamper the company's performance," Ross said.

While the airline still holds a dominant position in nine out of its 10 top markets, competition by low-cost carriers is intensifying. US Airways already faces an assault by Southwest Airlines Inc at about 25 of its locations.
The airline wants to create a low-cost carrier to compete with rivals such as Southwest and Delta Air Lines Inc's new Express unit.
